tutorials.title: What RendeerAlpha is
tutorials.tagline: An interface compiled ahead of time, and a backend in whatever language you already write.
tutorials.summary: The shape of the whole thing before any of the details: a TypeScript layout compiled into a flat binary blueprint, an application that loads it with no parser and no JavaScript engine, and a seam that sits at the state rather than at the pixels.

tutorials.title: Installing the engine
tutorials.tagline: One bring-up script, run once, that fills bin/ with everything an application needs.
tutorials.summary: What has to be on the machine, what the bring-up script does with it, and what lands in bin/ afterwards. The engine is a checkout you build once — after that a project in any language points at the result.

tutorials.title: Adding it to a project
tutorials.tagline: Four project shapes — and only one of them has a build system.
tutorials.summary: What sits beside your res/ folder in each language: a CMakeLists.txt for C++, a package.json for Node, a .csproj for C#, and nothing at all for Python.

tutorials.title: Your first interface
tutorials.tagline: A counter, a text field, and a button that asks the backend to do something.
tutorials.summary: Small enough to type in, and it exercises the whole path: a declaration both sides are generated from, a theme, a layout with bindings and handlers, and a backend answering a command.

tutorials.title: The layout language
tutorials.tagline: Constants, bindings and handlers — and a grammar small enough to compile into data.
tutorials.summary: What a .tsx layout may contain: the three kinds of value, the full expression grammar and the two rules it enforces, how sizing works, and the twenty-seven elements you have to build from.

tutorials.title: State and backends
tutorials.tagline: One declaration, four generated sides, and the same application in each language.
tutorials.summary: How res/state.ts becomes the C++ header, the Python module, the JavaScript module, the C# class and the layout’s type definitions — and what the same program looks like written against each of them.
